section.title: The Call of Wisdom and the Lure of Sin
section.sectionRationale: The first extended discourse of the book. A father's appeal to listen, verses 8 to 9, sets up a warning against violent men who entice the young, verses 10 to 19, and then Wisdom herself steps onto the street as a preacher, crying out in public and pronouncing judgment on those who refuse her, verses 20 to 33.
section.thesis: Two voices compete for the heart at the start of life: sinners who entice with quick, violent gain, and Wisdom who cries aloud in the open and warns that refusing her call has a real and lasting cost.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the parents' appeal to listen, verses 8 to 9; the enticement of violent men and its self destroying end, verses 10 to 19; and Wisdom's public call, refused, followed by the judgment that falls on those who refuse her, verses 20 to 33.

verses.text: Listen, my son, to your father's instruction, and do not forsake the teaching of your mother.
For they are a garland of grace on your head and a pendant around your neck.
My son, if {{chattaim|sinners}} entice you, do not yield to them.
If they say, "Come along, let us lie in wait for blood, let us ambush the innocent without cause,
let us swallow them alive like Sheol, and whole like those descending into the Pit.
We will find all manner of precious goods; we will fill our houses with plunder.
Throw in your lot with us; let us all share one purse."
My son, do not walk the road with them or set foot upon their path.
For their feet run to evil, and they are swift to shed blood.
How futile it is to spread the net where any bird can see it!
But they lie in wait for their own blood; they ambush their own lives.
Such is the fate of all who are greedy, whose unjust gain takes the lives of its possessors.

units.label: Wisdom's public call
units.note: she cries aloud, and is refused

verses.text: {{chokmah|Wisdom}} calls out in the street, she lifts her voice in the square;
in the main concourse she cries aloud, at the city gates she makes her speech:
"How long, O {{peti|simple ones}}, will you love your simple ways? How long will scoffers delight in their scorn and fools hate knowledge?
If you had repented at my rebuke, then surely I would have poured out my spirit on you; I would have made my words known to you.
Because you refused my call, and no one took my outstretched hand,
because you neglected all my counsel, and wanted none of my correction,
in turn I will mock your calamity; I will sneer when terror strikes you,
when your dread comes like a storm, and your destruction like a whirlwind, when distress and anguish overwhelm you.
Then they will call on me, but I will not answer; they will earnestly seek me, but will not find me.
For they hated knowledge and chose not to fear the LORD.
They accepted none of my counsel; they despised all my reproof.
So they will eat the fruit of their own way, and be filled with their own devices.
For the waywardness of the simple will slay them, and the complacency of fools will destroy them.
But whoever listens to me will dwell in safety, secure from the fear of evil."

chattaim.gloss: Sinners, those who habitually miss the mark of God's ways. Here they are organized and predatory, inviting the naive into violence and theft with the promise of shared plunder.

chokmah.gloss: Wisdom, personified in this passage as a woman who preaches publicly in the street and at the gates. She is not a private possession for the elite but a public voice offered to everyone who will listen.

peti.gloss: The simple or naive one, someone easily persuaded and without settled moral direction. Proverbs treats this state as dangerous but not hopeless, the simple can still turn and gain sense if they heed wisdom's call.

basic.context: Right after the book states its purpose, it shows that purpose in action. A father urges his child to listen to parental teaching, then warns against a gang of violent men who promise easy wealth through robbery and even murder. Then the passage shifts dramatically, Wisdom herself appears as a preacher in the public square, and when she is ignored, she promises that calamity will eventually come to those who refused her.
basic.hermeneutics: This is vivid, poetic warning literature, not a case study of one specific crime. The violent gang stands for any enticement to gain quickly through harming others, and Wisdom's public sermon stands for the many ordinary ways God's truth confronts us and is refused. The point is not that every sinner is a murderer, but that every temptation to sin promises gain and delivers ruin.
basic.originalLanguages: The chattaim, sinners, of verse 10 are not petty temptations but an organized invitation to violence, sharpening the warning. Wisdom, chokmah, is pictured as a public preacher, not a private secret. And those who refuse her are the peti, the simple, whose naivety becomes fatal only because they refuse correction, not because they were doomed from the start.
basic.typology: Wisdom's public cry that goes refused, followed by a judgment of being given over to one's own way, foreshadows the pattern Paul describes in Romans 1, God giving people over to what they insisted on choosing. It also anticipates Christ's own public preaching and weeping over a city that would not listen, Luke 19:41 to 44.
basic.christ: Wisdom stands in the street and cries out, offering herself freely, and is refused. Centuries later, Wisdom incarnate, Christ, stood in the temple courts and the streets of Jerusalem crying out the same offer, and wept over a city that would not come to Him, Matthew 23:37. He is both the wisdom that calls and, at the cross, the one who bears the judgment His hearers deserved for refusing.
basic.god: God is not hidden or stingy with wisdom; He sends it out publicly, urgently, repeatedly. Yet He is also just, He will not force anyone to listen forever, and He allows those who refuse Him to reap exactly what their own choices have sown.
basic.crossReferences: Romans 1:24 to 28 describes God giving people over to their own chosen path, echoing verses 31 to 32. Matthew 23:37 shows Christ crying over Jerusalem's refusal to be gathered. Luke 11:49 speaks of the wisdom of God sending prophets who are rejected. Galatians 6:7 states the same principle, a man reaps what he sows.
basic.oneStory: From the beginning, two calls compete for the human heart, the lure of quick and violent gain, and the public, patient call of wisdom. This passage's picture of a people who refuse wisdom until it is too late anticipates the whole Bible's story of a world that resists God's call, until Wisdom Himself, Jesus Christ, comes crying in the streets and finally dying so that those who turn to Him need never be turned away.

context.literary:
The poem is built as a contest of two speeches. In verses 11 to 14 the sinners speak, in five short rushes of 'come' and 'let us' that sound like a recruiting pitch: ambush, swallow, plunder, one purse. In verses 22 to 33 Wisdom speaks, at much greater length, and her voice is the larger one. The father sits between them, and his own advice in verses 10 and 15, 'do not yield' and 'do not walk the road with them,' is a refusal placed in the middle of an invitation. A reader is put in the position of the son, hearing two voices and made to choose.

The whole is also wrapped in a frame. It opens with 'Listen, my son,' verse 8, and closes with 'whoever listens to me,' verse 33. The Hebrew uses the same verb, shama, in both places, so the discourse begins and ends in the act of hearing, and everything between shows the cost of not doing it.

The gang's section turns on a cruel irony. They 'lie in wait for blood' in verse 11, and the sage answers that they 'lie in wait for their own blood' in verse 18. The word chinnam, without cause or in vain, appears twice, in verse 11 for their victims and in verse 17 for the foolish bird that sees the net. The innocent are ambushed for nothing, yet the plan itself is for nothing too.

Wisdom's address has the shape of a prophet's lawsuit: a question, 'How long,' verse 22; a lost offer, verse 23; the reasons introduced by 'because,' verses 24 to 25; the sentence, verses 26 to 28; the explanation, verses 29 to 31; and a verdict, verse 32. Then comes a single verse of promise, verse 33, which stands out because it is the only good word in the whole speech. Her place of speaking also climbs: street, square, the main concourse, the city gates, verses 20 to 21, a series that moves from the crowd to the court, so no one can say they did not hear.
context.historical:
The father speaks from a world in which a young man could be drawn into a band. Israel's history had plenty of examples: Abimelech hired worthless and reckless men to follow him, Judges 9:4, and the leaders of Shechem set up ambushes on the hilltops and robbed everyone who passed on the road, Judges 9:25. Hosea can compare a company of priests to raiders who lie in ambush and murder on the road to Shechem, Hosea 6:9. The pitch of verses 11 to 14 is therefore not a fantasy; it is the language of a gang, with a shared purse and the promise of 'all manner of precious goods.'

Against that stands the family. The father and the mother both teach, and the Hebrew word for the mother's teaching is torah, instruction, the word elsewhere used for God's law, verse 8. Their teaching is called a garland of grace and a pendant for the neck. Honour in Israel was worn: Pharaoh placed a gold chain around Joseph's neck when he made him ruler, Genesis 41:42. The father says that an obedient son wears his parents' words like an honour.

The places where Wisdom preaches are the places where Israel's public life happened. The city gate was where the elders sat, where Boaz settled the question of Ruth's redeemer, Ruth 4:1-2, and where the community brought a rebellious son, Deuteronomy 21:19. The prophets also stood at the gates to deliver God's word, as Jeremiah was told to do, Jeremiah 7:2. A sage who set Wisdom at the gates was giving her the standing of a prophet and a judge.

Wisdom's threat of calamity would have been heard against Israel's own history of invasion and exile. The 'storm' and 'whirlwind' of verse 27 are pictures of sudden military ruin, and a hearer in the exilic or postexilic era would have recognised in verse 24 a summary of what their ancestors did to the prophets, Jeremiah 7:13.
context.canonical:
Wisdom's public preaching is repeated and extended in the book itself. In Proverbs 8:1-5 she again stands on the heights, at the crossroads and beside the gates, and addresses the simple and the fools. In Proverbs 9:1-6 she builds a house, prepares a feast and sends out her maidservants to call the simple in. And Proverbs 9:13-18 sets a rival, the woman named Folly, who sits at her door and calls to the same passers by with the very same words, 'Whoever is simple, let him turn in here!' So Proverbs 1 introduces a contest that runs to the end of the opening section: two women, two houses, two invitations.

The passage also shares its idiom with the prophets, who report a God who called and was ignored. 'I called and you did not answer,' Isaiah 65:12; 'I have spoken to you again and again but you would not listen,' Jeremiah 7:13; 'just as I had called and they would not listen, so when they called I would not listen,' Zechariah 7:13. Isaiah 65:2 and Romans 10:21 speak of hands held out all day to an obstinate people, which reads like a commentary on 'no one took my outstretched hand.' The offer of Wisdom's spirit in verse 23 recalls the promise of God's Spirit poured out, Isaiah 44:3 and Joel 2:28.

The New Testament applies the passage to Christ. Jesus says that wisdom is vindicated by her actions, Matthew 11:19, and that the wisdom of God sent prophets and apostles, Luke 11:49. His lament over Jerusalem, 'how often I have longed to gather your children together... but you were unwilling,' Luke 13:34, breathes the same air. Paul describes the 'giving over' of those who refuse God in Romans 1:24-28, and says in Romans 3:15 that their feet are swift to shed blood, in words shared with Proverbs 1:16 and Isaiah 59:7.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The father wants the son to see the end of a plan before he enters it. The sinners' pitch is persuasive on purpose: it offers belonging, excitement and wealth, all at once, and it never mentions the price. The sage's counter is to replay the scheme from the other side. The bait is visible, the net is spread in plain sight, and the prey who walks into it is stupid, verse 17. The lesson is that sin makes a promise it cannot keep and that foolish people take a part in a trap that has their own names on it.

The second half is meant to make the son feel the weight of delay. Wisdom does not whisper. She calls in public, again and again, and she asks 'how long.' The intention is to jolt the simple out of the slow drift of putting decisions off, since the habit of refusing correction turns into a character, and character, once set, decides outcomes. The father does not want to threaten a son into obedience; he wants him to know what is at stake while there is still time to turn, verse 23.

The passage also meant to give parents standing. It opens by reminding the son that his father's instruction and his mother's teaching are part of Wisdom's own voice, the first place where she is heard. Home is where a person first meets the call, and the early habit of listening is the best defence against the later pull of the crowd.

Finally, the passage was meant to leave hope. The speech ends with a promise, verse 33, so that the one who takes the call to heart hears that the door is open, and nobody who listens is left outside.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The speech of the sinners in verses 11 to 14 is quoted, not endorsed. What the passage commands is plain: listen to your parents, verse 8; do not yield to enticers and do not walk their road, verses 10 and 15; and listen to Wisdom, verse 33. The pictures of the self-destroying gang and of calamity falling on the simple describe how sin generally works, a boomerang that comes back on the thrower, as the psalms also say of those who dig a pit, Psalm 7:15-16 and Psalm 9:15. They are not promises that every violent man will be repaid in kind within a lifetime, and the Old Testament knows that sometimes the wicked prosper, Psalm 73:3-5. The proverb teaches the shape of things as they tend to run under God's rule.

Two cautions follow in application. First, Wisdom's mockery in verse 26 belongs to her and to God, who alone knows when the day of calamity falls. Believers are told the opposite, 'do not gloat when your enemy falls,' Proverbs 24:17. Second, the passage does not turn parents or teachers into guarantors of a child's outcome: the father speaks and the son still chooses.

What carries over is the pattern of temptation. It arrives as an invitation from people, it promises quick gain, it hides the cost and it makes refusal feel like exclusion. A modern reader will not meet highwaymen, but fraud, exploitation of the weak and shared schemes for unjust profit all fit what verse 19 calls the greedy whose unjust gain takes their lives.

debates.question: Who is Wisdom in verses 20 to 33?

views.label: A personification, a literary figure for the teaching of the sages
views.case: The Hebrew often treats wisdom as a feminine noun and speaks of it as a person, as in Proverbs 3:13-18 and 9:1-6. Proverbs 7:4 tells the reader to call Wisdom 'my sister,' which shows the sages were comfortable with the device. On this reading Lady Wisdom is a poetic way of saying that the voice of right order is everywhere, in the street and the market.

views.label: A personification that speaks with the authority of God Himself
views.case: Verse 23 offers to pour out 'my spirit' and verse 28 declares that she will refuse to answer, prerogatives that belong to God. Luke 11:49 quotes 'the wisdom of God' sending prophets. On this reading she is God's own wisdom speaking through the sage, so that her rejection is a rejection of the LORD, verse 29.

views.label: A figure that points ahead to the Son of God
views.case: Many Christians, from the early centuries, have heard in her cry the voice of Christ, who calls in the open and weeps over those who will not come, Matthew 23:37, and Paul calls Christ the wisdom of God, 1 Corinthians 1:24. The reading depends on the New Testament's use of wisdom language and is strongest for Proverbs 8.

debates.bearing: Whatever the original author's precise categories, the three readings agree on what a hearer should do: to refuse Wisdom is to refuse God, and the New Testament shows that the call comes to its fullest and clearest form in Jesus.

debates.question: Is it true that those who call on Wisdom in verse 28 are not answered?

views.label: A real point of no return in the life of the persistent refuser
views.case: Hebrews 12:17 says that Esau, who sought the blessing with tears, found no ground for repentance, and Proverbs 29:1 warns that the person who remains stiff necked after much reproof will be broken without remedy. Habitual refusal can harden into a state that cannot be reversed, and the passage is a warning against reaching it.

views.label: A description of panic, not repentance
views.case: Verse 29 explains the silence: 'they hated knowledge and chose not to fear the LORD.' The cry of verse 28 is the cry of disaster, not of a changed heart, much as Hosea 7:14 says, 'They do not cry out to Me from their hearts.' The door is not closed to the penitent; it does not open to a bargain made in terror.

views.label: A rhetorical warning set within the larger promise of mercy
views.case: Isaiah 55:6-7 still says, 'Seek the LORD while He may be found,' and promises pardon to the one who returns. Wisdom speaks in proverbial language of a pattern, and the passage works to alarm the simple rather than to describe God's last word on any individual.

debates.bearing: The surest reading is the one that keeps all three texts in view: the warning is real, the hardened heart is the one that does not truly turn, and the whole book says 'today' to the reader who still hears the call, Hebrews 3:7-8.

debates.question: How can Wisdom 'laugh' at calamity, verse 26, if God is compassionate?

views.label: Judicial irony that echoes God's own laughter at rebels
views.case: Psalm 2:4 says the One enthroned in heaven laughs at the nations in rebellion. The scoffers of verse 22 mocked wisdom, and now the mockery returns. The laugh is the sound of justice, not of cruelty.

views.label: A rhetorical exaggeration that must be balanced by God's stated grief
views.case: Ezekiel 33:11 declares, 'I take no pleasure in the death of the wicked,' and Luke 19:41 shows Jesus weeping as He spoke of coming ruin. On this view the language of verse 26 is the sharpest way a sage can say that consequences will be real, and it does not tell us the temper of God.

debates.bearing: Both readings keep the main point. The laughter is not glee but the finality of a judgment that people brought on themselves, and it is spoken in order to be avoided, since verse 33 shows the same voice holding out safety.

study.originalLanguages:
The verbs of verses 23 to 32 make a pattern that English hides. In verse 23 Wisdom says, 'If you had repented at my rebuke,' using the verb shuv, to turn. In verse 32 the downfall of the simple is their meshuvah, their waywardness or turning away, from the same root. The one who turns toward the rebuke is received, and the one who turns away is lost: the book's whole teaching is packed into a pair of related words.

The word for rebuke, tokhachah, appears three times in this speech, in verses 23, 25 and 30, together with etsah, counsel, in verses 25 and 30. Both are the words of the sage's classroom, and Wisdom's accusation is that the simple refused the two things that would have made them wise, correction and advice. The refusal is described with strong verbs: they 'neglected' the counsel, they 'wanted none' of the correction, they 'despised' the reproof.

The verb in verse 28 for seeking earnestly, shachar, is built on the word for dawn and means to seek early and eagerly. Proverbs 8:17 uses it in the opposite direction: 'those who seek me early shall find me.' The same eager seeking that finds Wisdom in chapter 8 does not find her in chapter 1, because in chapter 1 it comes after the day of trouble has fallen and is not seeking at all in the sense of verse 29. The contrast makes the point that timing and motive matter.

The word nefesh, life or self, ties verses 18 and 19 together. The gang hope to take the lives of others, but the sage says that they 'ambush their own lives,' verse 18, and that unjust gain 'takes the lives of its possessors,' verse 19, both with nefesh. What they hunt is what they lose. The word for the net in verse 17 and the word for the bird, literally the master of wings, make a small riddle: any bird that can see the net stays clear of it, and the gang will walk into theirs with open eyes.

The verb in verse 10, al tove, 'do not yield,' is the verb of consenting or being willing. It is the same used when Moses commands that an enticer to idolatry must not be yielded to, Deuteronomy 13:8. The point is that enticement can only work with the hearer's consent, and the refusal is a matter of the will.

Verse 12 pictures the gang swallowing the innocent 'alive like Sheol,' which recalls Korah and his company, who went down alive into Sheol, Numbers 16:30-33, and the Pit, bor, is the usual word for the grave. In verse 20 the word for Wisdom is the plural chokmot, as in Proverbs 9:1, which many take as a plural of fullness or majesty, wisdom in all her forms. Verse 32 closes with shalvah, ease or complacency, a quiet word for the danger of a life that has never been challenged. In verse 33 the word for dwelling securely, betach, is the opposite of the dread that overwhelms the fool in verse 27.

typology.type: Wisdom crying in the street, verses 20 to 21
typology.fulfillment: Wisdom preaches in the open places of the city, and the Gospels give the same picture of Jesus. On the last and greatest day of the feast He stood up and called out in a loud voice, 'If anyone is thirsty, let him come to Me and drink,' John 7:37. He said, 'Come to Me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest,' Matthew 11:28, and the crowds heard Him in the streets, the hillsides and the temple courts. The escalation is that Wisdom's invitation is now made by the One whose wisdom it is, and it is made as an offer of rest and not only instruction. The type is limited in that the personified Wisdom of the proverb has no cross, while the call of Jesus will be sealed by His own death.

typology.type: The innocent ambushed without cause, verses 11 and 17
typology.fulfillment: The gang plans to 'ambush the innocent without cause,' the word chinnam of verse 11. The psalmist uses the same word of enemies who laid their net for him without cause, Psalm 35:7, and Jesus says that the Scripture is fulfilled, 'They hated Me without reason,' John 15:25. The chief priests and elders conspired to arrest Him covertly and kill Him, Matthew 26:3-4, and Judas admitted, 'I have sinned by betraying innocent blood,' Matthew 27:4. The proverb's pattern of the blameless victim and the plot for plunder comes to rest in the death of the one truly innocent person. The type falls short in that Christ was not caught in a net He did not see; He walked into it willingly, Luke 9:51, to turn the plot into redemption.

typology.type: Being given over to the fruit of one's own way, verses 28 to 31
typology.fulfillment: Wisdom's sentence is that those who refused her will 'eat the fruit of their own way.' Paul gives the same pattern at the scale of the nations: 'God gave them over in the desires of their hearts,' Romans 1:24, and again at verse 28, 'He gave them up to a depraved mind.' The deepest correspondence is the cross, because the same Greek verb is used of the Father in Romans 8:32, 'He who did not spare His own Son but gave Him up for us all.' The ones who refused Wisdom are handed over to the consequences of their choice, and the Son is handed over in their place. The type does not cover everything: Romans 1 describes a judicial abandonment that the gospel can still reverse for those who turn.

typology.type: Hands stretched out and not taken, verse 24
typology.fulfillment: Wisdom complains that no one took her outstretched hand. God says through Isaiah, 'All day long I have held out My hands to an obstinate people,' Isaiah 65:2, and Paul applies it to Israel, Romans 10:21. Jesus gives the same grief a face when He weeps over Jerusalem and says He would have gathered her children as a hen gathers her chicks, 'but you were unwilling,' Luke 13:34. The pattern finds its greatest expression in the cross, where the hands are literally stretched out in welcome and in suffering. The correspondence is real but guarded: the Gospels do not say that the cross was the open arms of Wisdom, and the image should be held as an echo and not as an equation.

study.christ:
Proverbs 1 speaks of Wisdom, the father and the sinners and does not name the Messiah. It leads to Christ by the paths the New Testament itself opens.

First, He is the one who makes Wisdom's cry in the open His own. Wisdom stood in the street and the square and at the gates; Jesus called out on the last great day of the feast, John 7:37, and said, 'Come to Me, all you who are weary and burdened,' Matthew 11:28. He identified His ministry with Wisdom's, saying that wisdom is vindicated by her actions, Matthew 11:19, and that the wisdom of God had sent prophets and apostles who would be killed and persecuted, Luke 11:49. In Matthew 23:34 He says, 'I am sending you prophets and wise men and teachers,' speaking in His own name what Luke attributes to the wisdom of God.

Second, His lament matches Wisdom's complaint. 'No one took my outstretched hand,' says verse 24. 'How often I have longed to gather your children together as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, but you were unwilling,' says Jesus, Luke 13:34. His words on the road into Jerusalem, 'If only you had known on this day what would bring you peace! But now it is hidden from your eyes,' Luke 19:42, echo Wisdom's 'how long' and her warning that the day of calamity will come. In both cases the God who warns is grieved by what He warns about.

Third, He faces the lure that Proverbs warns against and refuses. The devil showed Him all the kingdoms of the world and offered them without the cost of the cross, if only He would worship, Matthew 4:8-10. The temptation is the gang's pitch on a cosmic scale, quick gain by a forbidden road, and the Son answered with the word of God. Where the son of Proverbs is told, 'do not yield,' Jesus does not.

Fourth, He takes the place of the people who despised Wisdom. They are handed over to the fruit of their own way, verse 31, and the Father handed over His own Son for us all, Romans 8:32. The Innocent who was ambushed without cause, John 15:25, carried the judgment that belonged to those who refused the call, so that those who turn can live. The warning of the passage is never relaxed, but the cross means that the way back is still open: 'Today, if you hear His voice, do not harden your hearts,' Hebrews 3:7-8, and at the door of the Church He still stands and knocks, Revelation 3:20.

A caution is in order. Verses 20 to 33 should not be read as a prediction of Jesus' life, detail by detail, and the Proverbs do not say that Wisdom is the second person of the Trinity. The connection is that the New Testament sees in Jesus the full embodiment of what Wisdom's call was always trying to say, and the people who refuse Him repeat the pattern the passage describes.
study.god:
The God behind this passage is a God who calls loudly and in public. Wisdom is not an esoteric secret kept for an elite. She stands in the street and at the gates and speaks to everyone, and that is how God has chosen to make Himself known: openly, patiently and repeatedly, through parents, prophets, creation and, at the end, His Son. Paul says that God's kindness is meant to lead people to repentance, and that He is rich in tolerance and patience, Romans 2:4, and Peter that He is patient, not wanting anyone to perish, 2 Peter 3:9. The 'how long' of verse 22 is the voice of a God who has waited a long time.

He is also a God who gives. Verse 23 offers to pour out 'my spirit' and to make His words known. The picture is of generosity on the scale of a flood. This echoes the God of Isaiah who pours water on thirsty land and His Spirit on descendants, Isaiah 44:3. What He holds out is not a rulebook but a share in His own life and understanding.

He is a God of moral order, and the passage shows that order working in the open. The sinners are caught in their own trap, and the simple eat the fruit of their own way. Paul says the same thing in the plainest terms: 'Do not be deceived: God is not mocked. Whatever a man sows, he will reap in return,' Galatians 6:7. This is not the arbitrary violence of a vengeful deity but the structure of a world designed so that choices mean something. In that sense God's judgment is often the ratification of what people have already chosen, as Romans 1:24 describes it.

He is not mocked, and He is also not cold. The laughter of verse 26 has its counterpart in Psalm 2:4, and its counterweight in Ezekiel 33:11, where God swears that He takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked and pleads with them to turn. The same God who is angry at those who despise His word is the One who calls, 'Turn! Turn from your evil ways! For why should you die?' The passage is hard because it holds both together.

He is also the one who protects. Verse 33 closes with safety: whoever listens will dwell securely and be at ease without fear of evil. Proverbs 3:26 says why, 'the LORD will be your confidence and will keep your foot from the snare,' the very snare that caught the gang. The refuge is not found in a sealed life but in a listening one.

For worship, the passage asks us to hear God's voice in ordinary places, to respond while the call is still being made and to praise the One who is patient enough to cry out in the street rather than stay silent.

crossReferences.note: Moses tells Israel not to yield to a close friend or relative who secretly entices them to other gods. The same verb of consent stands behind 'do not yield' in Proverbs 1:10, linking the father's warning to the covenant's own refusal of the enticer.

Korah and his company went down alive into Sheol when the ground opened. The gang's boast to swallow the innocent alive, like Sheol, in verse 12 borrows this picture of sudden and complete death, and ironically the violent end they plan is the very end the sage says they will meet.
The nations fell into a pit of their making, and their feet were caught in the net they hid. It is the same law as Proverbs 1:17 and 18, that the trap set for others closes on the one who sets it.

Their feet run to evil and are swift to shed innocent blood. The prophet uses nearly the same words as Proverbs 1:16, and Paul in Romans 3:15 quotes the line to describe the human condition without God, so the gang's habits stand for a universal trait.

Folly sits at her door and calls the simple with the identical words Wisdom uses in 9:4, 'Whoever is simple, let him turn in here!' It shows that the choice in Proverbs 1 is a contest between two rival voices, and the guests of Folly are in the depths of Sheol.

God says He spoke again and again, called, and was not answered. The pattern of Proverbs 1:24 is repeated here as the reason for exile, so Wisdom's complaint becomes the prophets' charge against Israel.

They stopped their ears and made their hearts like flint, so when they called God would not listen. This is the clearest prophetic parallel to verse 28 and shows that the refusal of the call and the silence that follows is a pattern in Israel's story.

God held out His hands all day to an obstinate people and revealed Himself to those who did not ask. Together with Romans 10:21, it supplies the picture of the outstretched hand of Proverbs 1:24, and shows that God is always the one who reaches first.

Jesus longs to gather Jerusalem's children as a hen gathers her chicks, but they were unwilling. It is the closest New Testament echo of Wisdom's grief, and it gives the same mixture of tenderness and warning.

God gave them over to their desires and to a depraved mind. Paul describes a judgment that works by letting people have what they insisted on, which is the way Proverbs 1:31 describes eating the fruit of one's own way.

God is not mocked, and a person reaps what he sows. Paul uses the sage's moral logic in a gospel setting and points out that sowing to the Spirit reaps life, so the principle of Proverbs 1 is a call to sow well.

The One enthroned in heaven laughs and taunts the rebellious nations. It gives a parallel to the laughter of Wisdom in 1:26 and shows that the divine response to determined rebellion is not anxiety but sovereign judgment.

'Today, if you hear His voice, do not harden your hearts.' The urgency of Wisdom's 'how long' becomes the Spirit's word to the church, and the call remains open for as long as it is still called today.

study.oneStory:
The scene of Proverbs 1 is as old as the garden. A voice enticed with an offer of wisdom and gain, asked whether God had really said what He said, and drew the first people into a trap that closed on them, Genesis 3:1-6. The first murder, when Cain said, 'Let us go out to the field,' and killed his brother, Genesis 4:8, is the first ambush of the innocent, and by the time of the flood the earth was full of violence, Genesis 6:11. The gang of Proverbs 1 is a small portrait of the world after Eden.

In that world God has not been silent. Wisdom's public call is the story of the Old Testament in miniature: parents who taught, prophets who stood at the gates, and a God who sent them again and again, Jeremiah 7:13. Israel, who had been given the law that was meant to show their wisdom to the nations, repeatedly turned away, and the exile was the fruit of their way. Zechariah looks back and says that God called, they would not listen, and so when they called He would not listen, Zechariah 7:13. Isaiah says the same with the picture of hands stretched out all day, Isaiah 65:2.

The story reaches its center when Wisdom herself, in the person of the Son, comes into the same streets. He calls, He weeps, He is refused, and the city that would not hear is left to its desolation, Luke 13:34-35 and Luke 19:41-44. He is ambushed without cause, and the plot to arrest Him covertly and kill Him, Matthew 26:3-4, ends in the death of innocent blood. Yet the Father hands Him over for the very people who refused, Romans 8:32, and what the gang planned as an ending becomes the beginning of a rescue. Now God commands all people everywhere to repent, Acts 17:30, and the call goes on from every pulpit and every parent.

The Bible's last chapter keeps the call. The Spirit and the bride say, 'Come!' and the one who is thirsty may drink the water of life freely, Revelation 22:17. And the story ends with the safety that Wisdom promised. The deceiver is finally removed, there is no more death or mourning, and the gates of the city are never shut, Revelation 21:25. The city gates where Wisdom once cried and was not heard become the open gates of a place where no one needs to fear evil, and where those who listened live in safety with the God who called.

quiz.q: What do the violent men in verses 10 to 14 promise, and what do they actually deliver?

options.text: They promise quick, shared plunder, but their own scheme ends up destroying them.
options.note: Verses 18 to 19 make clear their violence recoils on themselves.

options.text: They promise wealth and deliver it without any cost.
options.note: The passage explicitly says their own greed takes their lives, verse 19.

options.text: They promise friendship, which they genuinely provide.
options.note: Their appeal to shared partnership, verse 14, is a cover for violence, not real friendship.

options.text: They promise wisdom in exchange for loyalty.
options.note: They promise material gain, not wisdom; this confuses their offer with what Wisdom herself offers later in the passage.

quiz.q: Where and how does Wisdom call out in verses 20 to 21?

options.text: Publicly, in the street, the square, and at the city gates.
options.note: The passage stresses that Wisdom's call is public and open to all, not hidden or exclusive.

options.text: Privately, only to a select few disciples.
options.note: The text emphasizes public, open proclamation, the opposite of a private, exclusive call.

options.text: Only through written scrolls circulated among scribes.
options.note: The passage pictures a spoken, public cry, not a written document.

options.text: Mainly inside the royal court.
options.note: The gate could include official business, but the emphasis is broader, the street and square, ordinary public life, not the court alone.

quiz.q: What happens to those who refuse Wisdom's repeated call, according to verses 24 to 31?

options.text: They are eventually left to reap the fruit of their own chosen way when calamity comes.
options.note: Verses 31 to 32 state this directly, they eat the fruit of their own way.

options.text: Wisdom keeps calling forever regardless of their response.
options.note: The passage instead describes a real turning point after persistent refusal, not endless, consequence free calling.

options.text: They are immediately destroyed the moment they first ignore her.
options.note: The passage describes a pattern of repeated refusal, verses 24 to 25, not instant destruction after one lapse.

options.text: Nothing changes for them either way.
options.note: The passage is explicit that real consequences follow persistent refusal.

quiz.q: What does the word peti, simple, describe in this passage?

options.text: One who is naive and easily led, a state that is dangerous but can still be corrected by heeding wisdom.
options.note: Verse 22 rebukes the simple for loving their simple ways, implying a choice, not a fixed condition.

options.text: Someone who is intellectually disabled and therefore blameless.
options.note: The term describes a moral and volitional state that Proverbs holds people responsible for, not a lack of capacity.

options.text: A title reserved only for children under a certain age.
options.note: The term applies broadly to anyone easily persuaded, not a strict age category.

options.text: Someone already fully wise but pretending otherwise.
options.note: This inverts the meaning; the simple genuinely lack settled wisdom, they are not wise people in disguise.

quiz.q: How does this passage anticipate Christ?

options.text: Wisdom's public cry and its refusal foreshadow Christ's open teaching and His weeping over Jerusalem's refusal.
options.note: Matthew 23:37 and Luke 19:41 to 44 draw exactly this parallel of public offer and tragic refusal.

options.text: It has no connection to the New Testament at all.
options.note: The New Testament itself draws directly on this pattern of a public call refused.

options.text: It shows Christ only as a stern judge with no patience.
options.note: The passage, like Christ's ministry, actually shows patient, repeated appeal before any judgment falls.

options.text: It teaches that wisdom is only for a spiritual elite.
options.note: The opposite is true, Wisdom cries in the open, offered to everyone who will listen, not an elite few.

questions: The violent men in this passage promise quick gain through harming others. What shortcuts are you tempted toward that promise a fast reward but would really cost you or someone else dearly?

Wisdom cries out in the open, in ordinary public places, not in secret. Where in your ordinary week is God's truth calling out to you plainly, whether through Scripture, a sermon, or a friend's honest word?
The passage warns against repeated refusal hardening into ruin. Is there a correction you have been putting off responding to, hoping to deal with it later?
Verse 33 promises safety and rest to whoever listens to wisdom. What would change in your sense of security this week if you truly believed that promise?
Wisdom's call anticipates Christ's own call, and His tears over those who refuse Him. How does knowing that Jesus still calls patiently change the way you want to respond to Him today?

translationNotes.note: Some manuscript traditions of Proverbs omit verse 16 as a later addition drawn from Isaiah 59:7, but its sense fits the surrounding warning and is retained in most translations, including the BSB.
The main concourse can also be rendered from the top of the wall, a reference to a public place where speakers could be heard by a crowd.
The Hebrew term rendered fool in this chapter denotes one who is morally deficient by settled choice, not merely lacking in intelligence.

meta.notes: BSB text fetched via the makor-scripture toolkit for Proverbs 1:8-33. the wording is otherwise unchanged and complete.
